_readme: P1 commissions (decided 2026-10-02): encounter -> help/diagnosis -> agreed terms -> staged work -> paid completion -> referral. Amounts are in aurei (1 = 25 denarii at AD 155 prices; scaled by the price level). Categories are P1 scene categories (Engineering, Personal, RomanLife, WorkEconomy, MachineMystery, CityHistory, Exploration, InstitutionsPolitics). Roman baseline first: Rome already has bronze force pumps; the inventor brings true, replaceable valve seats cut to a gauge. Amounts PROPOSED P1-05. P1 (2026-10-04): 'requires' (people.json syntax) gates when the work can come; 'fundingModel' may be Favor (no one pays) or ProfitShare; a work stage may name its own 'capability' and 'capabilityTo'; 'onComplete' gives regard, status and flags; 'referral' is optional and may be only a lead (no institution). Amounts PROPOSED P1-05, P1-14, P1-17, P1-19.

commissions.title: Cassianus's flooded cellar
commissions.clientRole: grain and oil merchant under the Aventine

encounter.text: Felix finds you at the smith's at first light. "There's a man under the Aventine with water to his knees," he says. "Cassianus. Grain and oil. His pump coughs more than it pumps. He'll feed you lunch to look at it, and that's all he's promised."

diagnosis.text: Cassianus's cellar smells of wet sacking. The pump is a good bronze force pump, two cylinders and a rocking beam, the kind the fire watch carries. The plungers are sound. Water spurts back past the leather flaps on every stroke: the seats are worn into ovals, and the last man who fixed them packed the gaps with wax. Cassianus watches you trace the leak with a finger. "Can you fix it, or do I buy another pump?"

terms.text: "Here is what I'll do," he says. "I buy the bronze and the leather. You make it pump. Three hundred denarii now, five hundred when my cellar is dry."

counter.acceptText: Cassianus counts on his fingers, then shrugs. "Seven hundred. If it pumps."
counter.standFirmText: "Five hundred," he says. "There are other men with clever hands." The offer stands as it was.
counter.walkText: Cassianus's face closes. "I asked a fair price and you asked a rich man's. I'll buy another pump." He sees you out himself.

commissions.declineText: You tell Cassianus you can't take it on. He nods and goes back to bailing.

work.text: You turn a new valve seat on the smith's lathe, true and flat, and cut the leather flap to sit on it. The first one leaks at one edge. The second holds.
The smith's apprentice learns to cut seats to your gauge. He spoils two, then makes four that fit. Cassianus has two more pumps at his warehouse by the river and wants them done the same way.
The cellar drains in an afternoon. Cassianus pours wine for the workmen on the wet steps, gives a cup to the Lares by the door, and pays you on the spot.

referral.text: Felix was at the drinking. "The men at Ostia have pumps too," he says, "and worse ones. Come out to one of our suppers sometime."

commissions.title: Aemilius's slipping hoist
commissions.clientRole: a warehouse owner at the Emporium below the Aventine

encounter.text: Felix finds you again, which he didn't have to. "Cassianus went elsewhere. Fine. Aemilius at the Emporium has a hoist that drops a load a week into the river. He's angrier than Cassianus and richer. Look at it before you say no."

diagnosis.text: Aemilius's hoist is a treadwheel crane, two men walking inside the wheel, and a good one. The pawl that should stop the drum running back is worn round, and the rope is spliced in three places. When a man stumbles in the wheel, the load runs away. Aemilius tells you about every load he has lost, with prices.

terms.text: "Two hundred now," Aemilius says, "four hundred when a month goes by without anything in the river. I pay for the iron and the rope. If I lose a load while you're working, it comes off the four hundred."

counter.acceptText: Aemilius snorts. "Five hundred and fifty. And nothing in the river."
counter.standFirmText: "Four hundred," Aemilius says. "Felix said you'd ask." The offer stands.
counter.walkText: Aemilius says he'll keep losing loads rather than be robbed on land, and does.

commissions.declineText: You tell Aemilius you can't. Felix shrugs; he has done what he can.

work.text: A new pawl forged hard and a ratchet cut deeper on the drum, so the wheel can't run back more than a hand's breadth. The smith grumbles at the hardness you ask for and makes it anyway.

A month of loads go up and nothing goes in the river. The men in the wheel sing a song with a rude verse about Aemilius. He pays you on the quay and pours a little wine for Portunus, god of harbors, before he counts the money.

referral.text: Felix was there when Aemilius paid. "The men at Ostia have hoists too," he says, "and pumps, and every kind of trouble. Come out to one of our suppers sometime."

commissions.title: Lollius's bilge pumps
commissions.clientRole: a shipper at Ostia with three hulls and leaking pumps

encounter.text: The shipper who complained at the guild supper finds you on the quay at Ostia. Lollius, three hulls, all of them wet. "Felix says you fixed the oil man's pump. Mine are worse. Come and look before I lose a cargo of grain to my own bilge."

diagnosis.text: Lollius's pumps are chain pumps and one bronze force pump, all clogged with sand and pitch. The force pump has the same oval seats as Cassianus's. The chain pumps are a different trouble: the buckets jam where the chain bends. Lollius stands over you the whole time and talks about the price of grain in Alexandria.

terms.text: "I pay for the bronze," Lollius says. "Four hundred now, eight hundred and fifty when all three ships go a week without bailing. And if they leak after, I tell every shipper on the river."

counter.acceptText: Lollius laughs. "A thousand and a hundred, then, and if they leak I'll have it back with interest."
counter.standFirmText: "Eight hundred and fifty," he says. "I can count as well as you." The offer stands.
counter.walkText: "Felix said you were reasonable," Lollius says. "Felix was wrong." He goes off to find a fitter who isn't.

commissions.declineText: You tell Lollius you can't take it. He shrugs and goes back to cursing his crew.

work.text: The smith's apprentice cuts three sets of seats to the gauge without you. You spend your days at Ostia rebuilding the chain pumps' bends so the buckets ride clear, while Lollius's crew watches and offers advice.

All three ships go out to Puteoli and back. Lollius's steersman pours a libation to Neptune at the stern before each one sails, and swears it is the libation that keeps them dry. Lollius pays you anyway.

referral.text: Lollius tells the shippers at the next supper. Two of them ask Felix where to find you; one asks what you charge, and whistles.

commissions.title: Pomponia's household fevers
commissions.clientRole: a widow with a household of forty in a Subura insula, one of Serenus's few paying patients

encounter.text: Serenus catches you at the fountain. "Pomponia has fever in her household again, the third summer running. She pays, which makes her rare. She wants to know why her people sicken and her neighbors' don't. I told her you count things."

diagnosis.text: Pomponia's insula has five floors: the family on the ground, freedmen above, slaves and lodgers in the garrets. Fever has been worst at the top. The household draws water from two places, the street fountain and a cistern in the yard that a freedman swears is sweeter. Pomponia follows you from room to room with a list of who has died.

terms.text: "I will pay a hundred and fifty denarii now and three hundred and fifty when you tell me something I can act on," Pomponia says. "Wax and tablets on my account. Serenus comes when he is called."

counter.acceptText: Pomponia sighs. "Five hundred, then. Serenus says you are worth it. Serenus says that about very few things."
counter.standFirmText: "Three hundred and fifty," she says. "I am a widow, not a fool." The offer stands.
counter.walkText: "Serenus will do it for less," Pomponia says, and he does, badly, without columns.

commissions.declineText: You tell Pomponia you can't take it on. Serenus doesn't look surprised.

work.text: A tablet for each floor, the same questions for every sick person: when it began, which water they drink, who nursed them. Serenus thinks the cistern is irrelevant and says so daily. The freedman who keeps the tablets on the third floor writes 'cistern' in the margin of every case.

Laid side by side, the tablets disagree with Serenus: the garrets drink only from the cistern, and the garrets are where the fever is. He reads them twice and says it proves nothing. He has the cistern drained anyway, 'for cleanliness', and finds a dead cat. Pomponia orders the household to the street fountain.

referral.text: Pomponia tells her sister, who tells her doctor, who tells Serenus that comparing households is a Greek affectation. Serenus repeats it to you with real pleasure.

commissions.title: Philippus's cold hot room
commissions.clientRole: keeper of the small baths behind the Circus Maximus

encounter.text: The bath-keeper Philippus has seen you in his warm room often enough to know your accent. "They say you fix water," he says. "My hot room hasn't been hot since the Kalends, and the customers are going to the big baths. Look at my pipes. Look, I said; nobody's paying yet."

diagnosis.text: The furnace is fine; the trouble is the water. Philippus's lead pipe from the aqueduct branch has been tapped by someone upstream and patched with clay where it splits. Half the flow goes to a fuller's yard he swears he doesn't know about. What reaches him is cold and too little for the boiler.

terms.text: "A hundred now," Philippus says, "three hundred when the hot room is hot. I buy the lead. And you never saw any fuller."

counter.acceptText: Philippus groans like a man being robbed. "Four hundred and fifty. If it's hot."
counter.standFirmText: "Three hundred," he says. "You can have a free bath every day for a year, which is worth more." The offer stands.
counter.walkText: "Bath-keepers don't get rich," Philippus says, "and neither will you, not from me." He hires a plumber who knows the fuller.

commissions.declineText: You tell Philippus you can't take it. He goes back to stoking a furnace that heats nothing.

work.text: You replace the split section with a new length of lead, sweat-soldered, and fit a bronze stopcock so the boiler fills and stops. The tap upstream you leave alone; it isn't your pipe. The hot room steams by the end of the month.

The hot room fills again: wrestlers oiling themselves, a lawyer rehearsing a speech in the steam, a hair-plucker whose customers yell. Philippus puts a little bronze Fortuna by the furnace door and gives you the first bath free.

referral.text: Philippus tells everyone in the warm room that the foreigner fixed his water. One of them owns a fuller's yard downstream, and doesn't look pleased.

commissions.title: Diodoros's broken jars
commissions.clientRole: who runs Cassianus's deliveries now, one-handed

encounter.text: Diodoros finds you after dark. "Cassianus takes a jar out of my pay for every one that breaks on the carts. Three this week. I can't pay you. I'm asking anyway."

diagnosis.text: The carts are fine; the jars are packed in loose straw and roll together on every rut of the Clivus. The drivers pack them the way they always have. The worst breakage is on the long axle cart, which bounces where the others sway.

terms.text: There is no money in it. Diodoros will owe you, and he is not a man who forgets what he owes.

counter.acceptText: Diodoros has nothing more to give.
counter.standFirmText: "I told you," Diodoros says. "I have nothing. It's a favor or it's nothing." The offer stands.

commissions.declineText: You tell Diodoros you can't. He nods as if he expected it, and goes.

work.text: A wooden frame for the cart bed with a hole for each jar, and a rope net over the top. You buy the wood yourself. The first load arrives with one jar cracked instead of five. The drivers call it a cage for chickens and use it anyway.

status.Diodoros: runs Cassianus's deliveries with jar frames on every cart, and keeps his pay

referral.text: Diodoros doesn't thank you. A week later a porter you don't know carries your tools across the city for nothing and says Diodoros sent him.

commissions.title: Vettius's fitting drawings
commissions.clientRole: a shipwright at Ostia who builds for three guild shippers

encounter.text: Felix brings Vettius the shipwright to a guild supper and seats him next to you on purpose. Vettius has two yards and every fitting in them is made by eye. "Felix says you draw things so another man can make them. Can you draw mine?"

diagnosis.text: Vettius's master shipwright keeps every fitting in his head and in his hands; his apprentices copy whatever he made last. The drawings Vettius has show shapes, not sizes. When the master is ill, the yard stops.

terms.text: "A hundred and twenty-five now," Vettius says, "four hundred when my second yard builds a hull from your drawings without my master in it. And a tenth of what I get for selling copies to the other yards, if anyone will buy them."

counter.acceptText: Vettius looks at Felix, who shrugs. "Five hundred and fifty, then."
counter.standFirmText: "Four hundred and the tenth," Vettius says. "The tenth may be worth more than both of us think." The offer stands.
counter.walkText: Vettius decides his master's hands are good enough, and they are, until they aren't.

commissions.declineText: You tell Vettius you can't take it. Felix looks disappointed and pours him more wine.

work.text: You spend two months in the yard with a wax board and a bronze rule cut to the shared foot, drawing every fitting the master makes, with its sizes. The master watches you the whole time and corrects one drawing in three, never kindly.
The second yard frames a hull from the drawings with the master in bed with gout. It isn't as good as his. It floats, and it fits the fittings, and the guild's shippers come to look at it.

referral.text: Copies of the drawings go round the Ostia yards within the year. Vettius pays your tenth twice, then stops, and says the copies people are selling aren't his.

commissions.title: The grain mill's burnt bearing
commissions.clientRole: owner of a grain mill on the Janiculum race

encounter.text: Aulus sends a boy down the hill: the third mill has burnt a bearing at the start of the grinding, and Statius the owner is shouting at everyone. "Bring your gauges," the message says. "And don't talk to Statius."

diagnosis.text: The bearing is burnt black and the shaft is scored. Statius's man greased it every week; the mill turns every day. The new wheel is bigger than the old one and nobody changed the bearing to match. Aulus says nothing while you work it out, then says "Yes."

terms.text: Statius, red in the face: "I pay when it grinds. Three hundred and seventy-five. Bronze on my account. Every day it doesn't turn I lose more than that, so don't take long."

counter.acceptText: Statius throws up his hands. "Five hundred and twenty-five! Just make it turn."
counter.standFirmText: "Three hundred and seventy-five," Statius says. "Aulus would do it for the bread." The offer stands.
counter.walkText: "Aulus," Statius shouts, "get me a man who doesn't haggle while my grain rots." Aulus fixes it himself in four days and doesn't speak to you for a month.

commissions.declineText: You tell Statius you can't. Aulus shrugs and starts on the bearing himself.

work.text: A wider shell, cut to your gauge, with a groove so the grease feeds itself, and a second one cut the same, to be kept on a peg by the wheel. Aulus makes Statius's man grease it every morning while he watches.

referral.text: The mill grinds through the season. Two other owners on the race ask Aulus who cut the spare shell. He tells them, which, for Aulus, is a speech.

commissions.title: Lollius's loading crane
commissions.clientRole: a shipper at Ostia, back with a bigger trouble

encounter.text: Lollius again, louder than before. "The pumps are perfect. Now the crane on my quay drops amphorae into the harbor. My men call it the god of breakage. Come and look; you know the way."

diagnosis.text: The crane is a big treadwheel on the quay, and the trouble is the jib: it swings when a load lifts, and the men steadying it with ropes let go when it swings hard. Two of them have lost fingers. Lollius knows exactly how many amphorae he has lost, and doesn't know the men's names.

terms.text: "Three hundred now, six hundred when a month of grain ships go through without a jar in the harbor," Lollius says. "I buy the timber and the iron."

counter.acceptText: Lollius laughs. "Eight hundred. You've learned to haggle at Ostia."
counter.standFirmText: "Six hundred," Lollius says. "Even for you." The offer stands.
counter.walkText: Lollius says he'll ask the Greek on the next quay, and does, and the Greek's crane works almost as well.

commissions.declineText: You tell Lollius you can't. He goes off to shout at his crane.

work.text: A slewing ring under the jib with a brake you can set with a lever, so the jib turns when the men want it to and not when the load does. The men steady the load with long poles instead of ropes wrapped round their hands.

A month of grain ships through Lollius's quay and not one jar lost. The men in the wheel still call the crane the god of breakage, but now they mean it fondly. One of them gives you a little clay figure of it.

referral.text: Lollius brags about his crane at the next supper. A shipper asks Felix whether the foreigner works for anyone who isn't a member. Felix says he works for whoever pays.

commissions.title: The race that loses its water
commissions.clientRole: owner of a grain mill on the Janiculum race

encounter.text: Aulus sends the same boy. This time it isn't Statius's bearing: the whole race leaks, and the three mills below get half the water they should. The owners are blaming each other. "Come up," the message says. "Bring nothing. Listen."

diagnosis.text: You walk the race with Aulus from the aqueduct branch to the last wheel. The boards are rotten at two joints and the upper owner has cut a notch to feed a garden. The water arrives at the third mill uneven, in surges, and the wheel stutters with it. Aulus points at each fault without a word.

terms.text: The owners agree, after an afternoon of shouting, to split it three ways: seven hundred and fifty denarii between them when the third wheel turns steady. Timber and lead on their account.

counter.acceptText: The owners grumble and agree to a thousand, a third each, and argue about whose third goes first.
counter.standFirmText: "Seven hundred and fifty," the oldest owner says. "Aulus would do it for less." The offer stands.
counter.walkText: The owners decide to fix it themselves, each his own stretch, which is how it got this way.

commissions.declineText: You tell the owners you can't take it. Aulus says nothing and starts on the joints himself.

work.text: New boards at the joints, sealed with pitch, a stilling pool above the third mill so the water arrives smooth, and a stone over the garden notch with Aulus sitting on it while the upper owner complains.
The three wheels turn together for a month. The owners hold a small sacrifice at the head of the race to the nymph of the spring, and argue during it about who paid for the lamb.

commissions.title: Comparing two households
commissions.clientRole: Iunia, who keeps a larger house on the Esquiline and a physician who disapproves of Serenus

encounter.text: Serenus, with a tablet in his hand: "Pomponia's sister wants the same counting done in her house. Her physician says it's nonsense. Which makes me want to do it more. She pays better than Pomponia, and complains less."

diagnosis.text: Iunia's house on the Esquiline is twice Pomponia's and better drained. Fever comes there too, but in the stables and the slaves' quarters by the old well, not upstairs. Her physician follows you about, saying everything you write down is obvious.

terms.text: "Two hundred now, four hundred and fifty when you show me something my physician didn't already know," Iunia says. "He'll be the judge of that, which is a joke."

counter.acceptText: Iunia smiles. "Six hundred. If he squirms."
counter.standFirmText: "Four hundred and fifty," she says. "I'm paying for the squirming already." The offer stands.
counter.walkText: Iunia decides her physician is cheaper.

commissions.declineText: You tell Serenus you can't take it. He goes alone, without the columns, and comes back with nothing.

work.text: Two houses side by side now, the same questions in both, kept by Iunia's steward and Pomponia's freedman without you there. The old well on the Esquiline matches Pomponia's cistern case for case. Iunia's physician says it proves nothing, then has the well closed.
Serenus reads both households to the Circle. Two physicians ask for blank tablets ruled the same way. He makes you rule them.

commissions.title: A senator's garden fountain
commissions.clientRole: for a senator's freedman who wants a fountain that plays tunes

encounter.text: Gaius sends Marcus with a message: a senator's freedman wants a garden fountain that sings like the ones in Alexandria, and Gaius has said yes without knowing how. "Come and tell him it can't be done," the message says, "or tell me how."

diagnosis.text: Hero of Alexandria wrote down how to make water sing: a cistern filling, air forced through pipes, little bronze birds that whistle in turn. Gaius has the book in a bad copy. The freedman wants four birds and an owl that turns its head. The water pressure in the garden is half what the book assumes.

terms.text: The freedman pays Gaius two hundred and fifty now and five hundred when the birds sing, and Gaius pays you half of it and buys the bronze. "Half," Gaius says, "because it's my name on the job."

counter.acceptText: Gaius looks at you for a long time. "Six hundred and fifty, then. Livia will say I'm a fool."
counter.standFirmText: "Half," Gaius says. "My name. My bronze." The offer stands.
counter.walkText: Gaius says he'll tell the freedman it can't be done, and does, and doesn't ask you for anything for a season.

commissions.declineText: You tell Gaius you can't. He tells the freedman the owl is impossible, and makes the birds himself, two of them, badly.

work.text: You redraw Hero's birds with sizes, for the pressure there actually is, and Gaius casts them. The first bird gargles. The third whistles. The owl turns its head once and sticks, and the freedman loves it anyway.

The fountain sings at the freedman's dinner, all four birds in turn, and the owl turns its head twice. The guests applaud the freedman. Nobody asks who made it. Gaius, at the back with the slaves, is grinning.

commissions.title: The drain under the Clivus
commissions.clientRole: of the vicus where Gaius's shop stands

encounter.text: After a storm the drain under the Clivus backs up, and the street runs knee deep with everything the drain should have carried away. The magistrates of the vicus, a baker and two freedmen, come to Gaius's shop to find you. "They say you know about water," the baker says. "The aediles say it's our drain."

diagnosis.text: The drain is old brick, built for half the houses now on the street, and choked where a new insula's foundations cut into it. The magistrates have a little money from the street's collection for the crossroads shrine, and none from anyone else.

terms.text: "We have four hundred," the baker says. "A hundred and fifty now, the rest when the street stays dry. Bricks from the shrine fund. Don't tell the Lares."

counter.acceptText: The baker counts the shrine money again. "Five hundred and fifty. The Lares can do without a new coat of paint."
counter.standFirmText: "Four hundred," the baker says. "There isn't any more. Look." He shows you the box. The offer stands.
counter.walkText: The magistrates go to the aediles instead, who promise to look at it next year.

commissions.declineText: You tell the magistrates you can't. The street floods again at the next storm.

work.text: A new run of drain round the insula's foundation, wider, with a trap where the gutters come in so the rubbish stops before it chokes the brick. The whole street turns out to watch, and the baker brings bread.
The next storm comes and the street stays dry. The magistrates paint a little notice by the crossroads shrine, thanking the Lares and, in smaller letters, the foreigner from Gaius's shop.
